statement: If the square on a straight line be five times the square on a segment of it, then, when the double of the said segment is cut in extreme and mean ratio, the greater segment is the remaining part of the original straight line.
heath_proof: For let the square on the straight line AB be five times the square on the segment AC of it, and let CD be double of AC; I say that, when CD is cut in extreme and mean ratio, the greater segment is CB. Let the squares AF, CG be described on AB, CD respectively, let the figure in AF be drawn, and let BE be drawn through. Now, since the square on BA is five times the square on AC, AF is five times AH. Therefore the gnomon MNO is quadruple of AH. And, since DC is double of CA, therefore the square on DC is quadruple of the square on CA, that is, CG is quadruple of AH. But the gnomon MNO was also proved quadruple of AH; therefore the gnomon MNO is equal to CG. And, since DC is double of CA, while DC is equal to CK, and AC to CH, therefore KB is also double of BH. [VI. 1] But LH, HB are also double of HB; therefore KB is equal to LH, HB. But the whole gnomon MNO was also proved equal to the whole CG; therefore the remainder HF is equal to BG. And BG is the rectangle CD, DB, for CD is equal to DG; and HF is the square on CB; therefore the rectangle CD, DB is equal to the square on CB. Therefore, as DC is to CB, so is CB to BD. But DC is greater than CB; therefore CB is also greater than BD. Therefore, when the straight line CD is cut in extreme and mean ratio, CB is the greater segment.
ai_proof_text:
13.2
**Statement:** If the square on a straight line be five times the square on a segment of it, then, when the double of the said segment is cut in extreme and mean ratio, the greater segment is the remaining part of the original straight line.

**Step 1.** Let AB be a straight line and C a point on it, so that AC is a segment of AB and CB the remaining part, and let the square on AB be five times the square on AC. Produce AB beyond B (P2). On the straight line so produced, cut off from C, in the direction of B, CE equal to AC, and from E, in the same direction, ED equal to AC (1.3). Then CD is double of AC, E is the middle point of CD, and D lies on the line on the same side of C as B. I say that, when CD is cut in extreme and mean ratio, the greater segment is CB.

**Step 2.** Since the straight line AB is cut at C, the square on AB is equal to the squares on AC, CB together with twice the rectangle contained by AC, CB (2.4).

**Step 3.** By hypothesis the square on AB is five times the square on AC, that is, four times the square on AC together with the square on AC. Therefore the squares on AC, CB together with twice the rectangle AC, CB are equal to four times the square on AC together with the square on AC (CN1). Subtracting the square on AC from each, the square on CB together with twice the rectangle AC, CB is equal to four times the square on AC (CN3).

**Step 4.** Since CD is cut at E, the square on CD is equal to the squares on CE, ED together with twice the rectangle contained by CE, ED (2.4). But CE and ED are each equal to AC, so each of the squares on CE, ED and the rectangle CE, ED is equal to the square on AC; hence the square on CD is four times the square on AC. Therefore the square on CB together with twice the rectangle AC, CB is equal to the square on CD (CN1).

**Step 5.** Since CD is cut at E, the rectangle contained by CB, CD is equal to the rectangles contained by CB, CE and by CB, ED (2.1); and since CE, ED are each equal to AC, each of these rectangles is equal to the rectangle AC, CB. Therefore the rectangle CD, CB is twice the rectangle AC, CB, and so, by Step 4, the square on CB together with the rectangle CD, CB is equal to the square on CD (CN1).

**Step 6.** I say that CB is less than CD. For, if not, CB is either equal to or greater than CD. If CB is equal to CD, the square on CB is equal to the square on CD. If CB is greater than CD, cut off from CB the part CF equal to CD (1.3); then the square on CB is equal to the squares on CF, FB together with twice the rectangle CF, FB (2.4), so that the square on CB is greater than the square on CF, that is, than the square on CD (CN5). In either case the square on CB is not less than the square on CD; hence the square on CB together with the rectangle CD, CB is greater than the square on CD (CN5). But by Step 5 it is equal to the square on CD: which is impossible. Therefore CB is less than CD; and since B and D lie on the same side of C, the point B lies between C and D, so that CD is cut at B into the segments CB, BD.

**Step 7.** Since CD is cut at B, the rectangle contained by CD, CB together with the rectangle contained by CD, BD is equal to the square on CD (2.2).

**Step 8.** Therefore, by Steps 5 and 7, the square on CB together with the rectangle CD, CB is equal to the rectangle CD, CB together with the rectangle CD, BD (CN1). Subtracting the rectangle CD, CB from each, the square on CB is equal to the rectangle contained by CD, BD (CN3).

**Step 9.** Since the rectangle contained by the extremes CD, BD is equal to the square on the mean CB, the three straight lines CD, CB, BD are proportional: as CD is to CB, so is CB to BD (6.17).

**Step 10.** Since CB is a part of CD, CD is greater than CB (CN5). And in the proportion CD : CB = CB : BD the first term CD is greater than the third term CB; therefore the second term CB is greater than the fourth term BD (5.14).

**Step 11.** Therefore the straight line CD, which is double of the segment AC, is so cut at B that, as the whole CD is to the greater segment CB, so is CB to the less segment BD; that is, CD is cut in extreme and mean ratio at B (D6.3), and its greater segment CB is the remaining part of the original straight line AB. Q.E.D.
